_comment: Hand-written items for topics the extractor cannot serve. In this source those are tables whose row meaning lives in arrow glyphs with no Unicode mapping, so the text layer holds only the bare figure. Each entry is transcribed from the page image named in sourceNote; a topic listed here replaces the extractor's output for that topic. Verify against the figure in the reader before trusting a number.

preflight-fuel.sourceNote: Transcribed from public/source/reference-v7-1/page-25.webp, CASR 91.455 and Part 91 MOS 19.02.

items.prompt: Fuel Requirements — MTOW 5700 kg or below, day VFR: final reserve and contingency fuel?
items.answer: 30 minutes final reserve; no contingency fuel

items.prompt: Fuel Requirements — MTOW 5700 kg or below, night VFR: final reserve and contingency fuel?
items.answer: 45 minutes final reserve; no contingency fuel

items.prompt: Fuel Requirements — MTOW 5700 kg or below, IFR: final reserve and contingency fuel?
items.answer: 45 minutes final reserve; no contingency fuel

items.prompt: Fuel Requirements — turbojet, or turboprop above 5700 kg, IFR or VFR: final reserve and contingency fuel?
items.answer: 30 minutes final reserve; 5 per cent contingency fuel

items.prompt: Fuel Requirements — piston above 5700 kg, IFR or VFR: final reserve and contingency fuel?
items.answer: 45 minutes final reserve; 5 per cent contingency fuel

alternates-suitability.sourceNote: Transcribed from public/source/reference-v7-1/page-26.webp, Part 91 MOS 8.07 and AIP ENR 1.1 Para 10.7.1.2.

items.prompt: Suitability of Alternates — an aerodrome may be nominated as a destination alternate only if it is what three things?
items.answer: Suitable as a planned destination aerodrome for the flight; not itself an aerodrome for which the aircraft would require a destination alternate; and not a helideck
distractors: Suitable as a planned destination; served by an instrument approach; and not a helideck
Suitable as a planned destination; within one hour flight time; and not a helideck
Suitable as a planned destination; not itself requiring an alternate; and served by PAL

items.prompt: Suitability of Alternates — Part 91 aircraft: when must a destination alternate be planned for an IFR flight by night?
items.answer: When the planned destination is not served by an instrument approach procedure, or is served by one or more that the pilot is unable to conduct

items.prompt: Suitability of Alternates — IFR alternate minima where the pilot can conduct an instrument approach at the alternate?
items.answer: The alternate minima published on the chart.

items.prompt: Suitability of Alternates — IFR alternate minima where there is no instrument approach, or the pilot cannot conduct it?
items.answer: By day only: the lowest safe altitude for the final route segment plus 500 ft, and a visibility of 8 km.
distractors: By day only: the lowest safe altitude for the final route segment plus 1000 ft, and a visibility of 8 km
By day or night: the lowest safe altitude for the final route segment plus 500 ft, and a visibility of 8 km
By day only: the lowest safe altitude for the final route segment plus 500 ft, and a visibility of 5000 m

items.prompt: Suitability of Alternates — what applies if navigation uses a GNSS receiver certified only to (E)TSO C-129?
items.answer: Navigation to a destination alternate must be planned using a navigation system other than GNSS.
distractors: Navigation to the alternate may still be planned using that GNSS
An alternate is not required if the GNSS is serviceable
The alternate must be served by an ILS

enroute-deviations.sourceNote: Transcribed from public/source/reference-v7-1/page-37.webp, AIP ENR 1.1 Para 4.6.2. These are the deviations the pilot must immediately notify ATC of.

items.prompt: Deviations in Controlled Airspace — when must the pilot notify ATC?
items.answer: Immediately, for any of the listed navigation deviations.
distractors: Within 5 minutes of the deviation being detected
On first contact with the next sector
Only if the deviation exceeds twice the tolerance

items.prompt: Deviations in Controlled Airspace — NDB tolerance?
distractors: Half-scale deflection

items.prompt: Deviations in Controlled Airspace — LOC/VOR tolerance?
items.answer: Half-scale deflection
distractors: Full-scale deflection
± 2 NM

items.prompt: Deviations in Controlled Airspace — RNP/RNAV tolerance?
items.answer: Outside the prescribed RNP/RNAV value

items.prompt: Deviations in Controlled Airspace — DME tolerance?
items.answer: ± 2 NM
distractors: ± 1 NM
± 5 NM
Half-scale deflection

items.prompt: Deviations in Controlled Airspace — visual tolerance?
items.answer: 1 NM
distractors: 2 NM
5 NM
Within the circling area

items.prompt: Visual Approaches issued by ATC — by day, when may one be issued?
items.answer: Within 30 NM; continuous visual reference to ground or water; visibility 5000 m
distractors: Within 30 NM; clear of cloud; visibility 5000 m
Within 50 NM; continuous visual reference to ground or water; visibility 5000 m
Within 30 NM; continuous visual reference to ground or water; visibility 8 km

items.prompt: Visual Approaches issued by ATC — by night, when may one be issued?
items.answer: Within 30 NM; continuous visual reference to ground or water; visibility 5000 m; and, if being vectored, assigned MVA and given heading or tracking instructions to intercept final or to position within the circling area

items.prompt: Visual Approaches issued by ATC — what does night add over day?
items.answer: The vectoring condition: if being vectored the aircraft must be assigned MVA and given heading or tracking instructions to intercept final or to position within the circling area.
distractors: Nothing — the day and night conditions are identical
A reduced range of 15 NM instead of 30 NM
A requirement for the aerodrome to be in sight

items.prompt: Go Around in VMC — going around from a visual approach, what must the aircraft do?
items.answer: Except as specified in ERSA for specific locations, initially climb on runway track, remain visual and await instructions from ATC. If obstacles on runway track cannot be cleared, the aircraft may turn.
distractors: Turn immediately onto the published missed approach track and climb
Climb on runway track and carry out the published instrument missed approach
Enter the circuit from upwind and await instructions

items.prompt: Go Around in VMC — unable or unwilling to land from an instrument approach in VMC: what applies?
items.answer: Carry out the published instrument missed approach procedure for the approach being flown, unless ATC directs otherwise.
distractors: Climb on runway track, remain visual and await ATC instructions
Enter the circuit from upwind and re-position for another approach
Carry out the published missed approach only if ATC directs it

items.prompt: Go Around in VMC — at a Class D aerodrome with parallel runways and contra-rotating circuits, what must the pilot do?
items.answer: Commence climb to circuit altitude; position on the active side and parallel to the nominated duty runway while maintaining separation from other aircraft; and follow ATC instructions or re-enter the circuit from upwind

items.prompt: Go Around in VMC — what does the author advise if there is doubt about which procedure applies?
items.answer: Seek clarification from ATC. Confusion could arise from a clearance such as "cleared visual approach runway 01, track via the ILS".

approach-visual-requirements.sourceNote: Transcribed from public/source/reference-v7-1/page-52.webp, AIP ENR 1.5 Para 1.14. The source table is split Day / Night; the day-only criteria are exactly what a flat text extraction loses.

items.prompt: Visual Approach Requirements — by day, when need the pilot not commence, or may discontinue, an IAP?
items.answer: Within 30 NM; clear of cloud; in sight of ground or water; visibility 5000 m or the aerodrome in sight
distractors: Within 30 NM; clear of cloud; in sight of ground or water; visibility 8 km
Within 50 NM; clear of cloud; in sight of ground or water; visibility 5000 m
Clear of cloud; in sight of ground or water; visibility 5000 m

items.prompt: Visual Approach Requirements — by night, when need the pilot not commence, or may discontinue, an IAP?
items.answer: Clear of cloud; in sight of ground or water; visibility 5000 m. There is no 30 NM provision by night, and the aerodrome being in sight does not substitute for the visibility.

items.prompt: Visual Approach Requirements — which day provisions do NOT carry over to night?
items.answer: The 30 NM provision, and accepting the aerodrome in sight in place of 5000 m visibility
distractors: Being clear of cloud, and in sight of ground or water
The 5000 m visibility, and being clear of cloud
None — the day and night requirements are the same

items.prompt: Visual Approach Requirements — in CTA, what altitude must be maintained?
items.answer: Not less than 500 ft above the lower limit of the CTA, unless clearance has been received to depart and re-enter CTA.
distractors: Not less than 1000 ft above the lower limit of the CTA
Not less than 500 ft above the lower limit of the CTA, with no exception
Not less than the LSALT for the segment

items.prompt: Visual Approach Requirements — by night, what is the minimum altitude outside that CTA case?
items.answer: LSALT/MSA, the DGA step, or the last assigned altitude if being vectored.
distractors: 500 ft above the lower limit of the CTA in all cases
LSALT/MSA only — a DGA step may not be used
The last assigned altitude in all cases

items.prompt: Visual Approach Requirements — by day, how long must track or heading on the authorised route be maintained?
items.answer: Until within 5 NM.
distractors: Until within 3 NM
Until within the circling area
Until within 10 NM

items.prompt: Visual Approach Requirements — by night, how long must track or heading on the authorised route be maintained?
items.answer: Until within the circling area; or within 3 NM with the aerodrome in sight if there is no IAP, the pilot is not authorised to use it, or the flight is VFR.

items.prompt: Visual Approach Requirements — by night, what guidance distances allow the approach to continue?
items.answer: 5 NM on PAPI; 7 NM on PAPI for an ILS runway; 10 NM on glideslope; or 14 NM for YSSY runways 16L and 34L established not below glideslope and less than full scale azimuth deflection

items.prompt: Navigation Requirements Under the IFR — by what three means may an aircraft be navigated?
items.answer: An approved area navigation system meeting the performance requirements of the intended airspace or route; a radio navigation system or systems; or visual reference to the ground or water by day

items.prompt: Navigation Requirements Under the IFR — navigating by radio navigation aids: what tracking error allowance applies, and what is the maximum interval between fixes?
items.answer: After allowing for tracking errors of ± 9° from the last positive fix, the aircraft must come within the rated coverage of a radio aid usable as a fix. The maximum time interval between fixes must not exceed two hours.
distractors: ± 5° from the last positive fix, with a maximum of two hours between fixes
± 9° from the last positive fix, with a maximum of one hour between fixes
± 9° from the last positive fix, with no maximum interval between fixes

items.prompt: Navigation Requirements Under the IFR — when may visual reference to the ground or water be used?
items.answer: By day, on route segments where suitable enroute radio navigation aids are not available, provided weather permits flight in VMC and the visual position fixing requirements can be met.
distractors: By day or night, where suitable enroute aids are not available
By day, anywhere along the route at the pilot's discretion
By day, where aids are unavailable, provided the aircraft remains within 50 NM of departure

items.prompt: Navigation Requirements Under the IFR — the author's rule of thumb for distance able to be flown?
items.answer: 6.66 × rated coverage. The two-hour maximum between fixes still applies, and a fix can be achieved before station passage with GNSS or a co-located DME within rated coverage.
distractors: 3.33 × rated coverage
1.23 × rated coverage
6.66 × rated coverage, with no time limit between fixes

alternates-triggers.sourceNote: Transcribed from public/source/reference-v7-1/page-27.webp, page-28.webp and page-29.webp. Part 91 MOS 8.04/8.06, AIP ENR 1.1 Para 10.7.2. The source's own mnemonic is ACVWPLS — Alternates Could Very Well Prove Life Savers.

items.prompt: Alternate weather — over what window must the forecast conditions be considered?
items.answer: Arrival during the currency of, or up to 30 minutes prior to the forecast commencement of, the listed conditions.
distractors: Arrival during the currency of, or up to 60 minutes prior to the forecast commencement

items.prompt: Alternate weather — cloud: what triggers an alternate?
items.answer: More than SCT below the alternate minimum.
distractors: More than BKN below the alternate minimum
Any cloud below the alternate minimum
More than SCT below the landing minimum

items.prompt: Alternate weather — visibility: what two cases trigger an alternate?
items.answer: Visibility less than the alternate minimum; or visibility greater than the alternate minimum but the forecast endorsed with at least a 30 per cent probability of fog, mist, dust or any other phenomenon restricting visibility below the alternate minimum
distractors: Visibility less than the alternate minimum only
Visibility less than the alternate minimum, or any PROB endorsement at all
Visibility less than the landing minimum, or a 40 per cent probability of restriction

items.prompt: Alternate weather — wind: what triggers an alternate, and what must be considered with it?
items.answer: A crosswind or tailwind component more than the maximum for the aircraft. Wind gusts must be considered.
distractors: A crosswind component more than the maximum for the aircraft; gusts are disregarded
A total wind of 25 kt or more, gusts included
A tailwind component only; crosswind is covered by the landing minima

items.prompt: Alternate weather — which flights are excepted from the cloud, visibility and wind requirement?
items.answer: Flights operating under the VFR by day within 50 NM of the point of departure.
distractors: Flights under the VFR by day within 30 NM of the point of departure
Flights under the VFR by day or night within 50 NM of the point of departure
Flights under the IFR within 50 NM of the point of departure

items.prompt: Alternate weather — thunderstorms: how much holding fuel for a forecast endorsed INTER?
items.answer: 30 minutes
distractors: 60 minutes
45 minutes
15 minutes

items.prompt: Alternate weather — thunderstorms: how much holding fuel for a forecast endorsed TEMPO?
items.answer: 60 minutes
distractors: 30 minutes
45 minutes
90 minutes

items.prompt: Alternate weather — what probability of a thunderstorm or associated severe turbulence triggers an alternate?
items.answer: A forecast of the event, or a forecast of at least a 30 per cent probability of it.
distractors: At least a 40 per cent probability
At least a 20 per cent probability

items.prompt: Alternate weather — what applies when no aerodrome forecast is available?
items.answer: The pilot in command must make provision for a suitable alternate that has an available forecast.
distractors: The area forecast may be used instead, with minima increased by 50 ft

A PROB30 must be assumed and holding fuel carried

items.prompt: Alternate lighting — when aerodrome lighting is required and PAL is not used, over what periods must it be arranged to operate?
items.answer: Departure: from 10 minutes before departure to at least 30 minutes after take-off. Arrival: from at least 30 minutes before ETA until landing and taxiing has been completed
distractors: Departure: 30 minutes before to 10 minutes after take-off. Arrival: 10 minutes before ETA until landing
Departure: 10 minutes before to 30 minutes after take-off. Arrival: 15 minutes before ETA until landing

items.prompt: Alternate lighting — a PAL aerodrome may be nominated as an alternate with no responsible person in attendance if the aircraft has what?
items.answer: Dual VHF; or single VHF and HF, carrying 30 minutes holding fuel to allow for alerting ground staff if the aircraft's VHF fails
distractors: Dual VHF only

Dual VHF and HF, with no additional fuel requirement

alternates-special-minima.sourceNote: Transcribed from public/source/reference-v7-1/page-29.webp and page-30.webp. Part 91 MOS 8.08, AIP ENR 1.5 Para 6.2.

approach-qnh.sourceNote: Transcribed from public/source/reference-v7-1/page-42.webp, Part 91 MOS 14.03 and AIP ENR 1.5 Para 5.3.

approach-missed.sourceNote: Transcribed from public/source/reference-v7-1/page-55.webp, Part 91 MOS 15.11 and 1.07, AIP ENR 1.5 Paras 1.9.1 and 1.11. The source's mnemonic is "So Not Visual ROFL".

items.prompt: Missed Approaches — the source's "So Not Visual ROFL" mnemonic covers which six triggers?
items.answer: Straight-in landing cannot be effected; Not visual at the DA/RA height or MAPT; RAIM warning or loss of RAIM; Outside navigational tolerance in the final segment; Failure or suspect aid below MSA; Lost visual reference during circling

distractors: Unless the aerodrome is in sight by the MAPT

distractors: A RAIM warning at any point after departure
A RAIM warning after the FAF only

items.prompt: Missed Approaches — "F": when does a failed or suspect aid require a missed approach?

distractors: Failure of an aid at any altitude

items.prompt: Speed Definitions — what is VMCA, and which radial marks it?
items.answer: Minimum control speed, air — the red radial. The minimum speed at which it is possible to maintain directional control of the aircraft with the critical engine inoperative.

items.prompt: Speed Definitions — on what conditions is VMCA determined?
items.answer: Critical engine inoperative; live engine at take-off power; landing gear retracted; a maximum of 5 degrees bank towards the live engine; propeller feathered (only for aircraft with automatic feathering devices)

items.prompt: Speed Definitions — what is VMCG?
items.answer: Minimum control speed, ground. The minimum speed, whilst on the ground, at which it is possible to maintain direction using only aerodynamic controls — critical engine inoperative, live engine at take-off power.

items.prompt: Speed Definitions — what is VSSE, and what is it for?
items.answer: Single engine safety speed: the speed below which intentional simulated engine failures should not be conducted. A manufacturer-stated speed intended to provide a margin above VMCA.

items.prompt: Speed Definitions — what is VYSE, and which radial marks it?
items.answer: Single engine best rate of climb speed — the blue radial. The speed at which the best rate of climb can be achieved with the critical engine inoperative.

items.prompt: Speed Definitions — on what conditions is VYSE determined?
items.answer: Critical engine inoperative; live engine at take-off power; landing gear retracted

items.prompt: Speed Definitions — which radials mark VMCA and VYSE?
items.answer: VMCA is the red radial; VYSE is the blue radial
distractors: VMCA is the blue radial; VYSE is the red radial

items.answer: A maximum of 5 degrees towards the live engine

items.prompt: Aircraft Equipment — what must be fitted for aeroplane IFR flight?
items.answer: Approved GNSS; AI; ASI; ALT; VSI; turn and slip; DG; compass; OAT; clock

items.prompt: Aircraft Equipment — what is required of the ASI and the pressure instruments?
items.answer: Pitot heat on at least one ASI. The ASI, ALT and VSI need an alternate static source or a balanced pair of flush static ports.

items.prompt: Aircraft Equipment — what power supply do the AI, turn and slip, and DG require?
items.answer: Primary and alternate power supply, unless independent of the turn and slip or a second AI is required. There must also be equipment showing adequate power supply to the gyroscopic instruments.

items.prompt: Aircraft Equipment — when is slip alone acceptable instead of turn and slip, and may the clock be worn?

items.prompt: Altitude alerting — which aircraft must be fitted with altitude alerting equipment for an IFR flight?
items.answer: A piston-engine aircraft in controlled airspace above FL 150; an unpressurised turbine-engine aircraft in controlled airspace above FL 150; a pressurised turbine-engine aircraft in any controlled airspace

items.prompt: Altitude alerting — what must the equipment do?
items.answer: Include an assigned altitude indicator; alert the flight crew when approaching a preselected altitude; alert the flight crew, including by an aural warning, if deviating from a preselected altitude

items.prompt: Altitude alerting — what applies to any other aircraft under the IFR in controlled airspace?

items.prompt: Flight with inoperative equipment — when may required equipment be inoperative?

items.prompt: Cockpit and cabin lighting — what is required?
items.answer: Equipment illumination including checklists and documents; compatible with each item of equipment; from a normal position all placards and instrument markings readable with eyes shielded from direct and reflected light; variable intensity; cabin lighting for seatbelt, oxygen normal and emergency exits; an independent portable light for each flight crew member

items.prompt: Anti-collision lights — what satisfies the requirement?

items.prompt: Altimeter Checks — when must a pre-flight altimeter accuracy check be conducted?
items.answer: Whenever an accurate QNH is available and the aircraft is at a known elevation, at some point prior to take-off.

items.prompt: Altimeter Checks — with an accurate QNH set, what must an IFR altimeter read, and at what error is it unserviceable?
items.answer: It should read the nominated elevation to within 60 ft. An error in excess of ± 75 ft means the altimeter must be considered unserviceable.
distractors: Within 75 ft, and unserviceable beyond ± 100 ft
Within 50 ft, and unserviceable beyond ± 75 ft
Within 60 ft, and unserviceable beyond ± 100 ft

items.prompt: Altimeter Checks — two altimeters required, and the remaining one is in error by between 60 and 75 ft. What is permitted?
items.answer: One altimeter must read the nominated elevation to within 60 ft. With the remaining altimeter between 60 and 75 ft, flight under the IFR to the first point of landing, where the altimeter can be re-checked, is approved. If it then shows an error in excess of 60 ft on the second check, it must be considered unserviceable for flight under the IFR.

items.prompt: Altimeter Checks — two altimeters fitted but only one required for the category of operation. What applies?
items.answer: The aircraft may continue to operate under the IFR provided one altimeter reads the nominated elevation to within 60 ft. Should the remaining altimeter be in error by more than 75 ft it must be placarded unserviceable and the maintenance release appropriately endorsed.

items.prompt: Altimeter Checks — only one altimeter fitted, in error by between 60 and 75 ft. What is permitted?
items.answer: Flight under the IFR to the first point of landing, where the accuracy can be re-checked, is approved. If the second check shows an error in excess of 60 ft the altimeter is to be considered unserviceable for flight under the IFR.

items.prompt: Altimeter Checks — what tolerance applies to a VFR altimeter?
items.answer: With an accurate QNH set it should read site elevation to within 100 ft, or 110 ft at test sites above 3,300 ft, to be accepted as serviceable by the pilot.
distractors: Within 100 ft, or 110 ft at test sites above 5,000 ft
Within 75 ft, or 100 ft at test sites above 3,300 ft
Within 110 ft, or 120 ft at test sites above 3,300 ft

items.prompt: Altimeter Checks — if the first check indicates an altimeter is unserviceable, what may the pilot do?
items.answer: Conduct a further check at another location on the same airfield — for example the first on the tarmac and the second at the runway threshold — to determine serviceability.

items.answer: Continuously in a position from which a descent to a landing on the intended runway can be made at a normal rate of descent using normal flight manoeuvres, allowing touchdown within the touchdown zone of the runway of intended landing.

items.prompt: DME or GNSS Arrivals — what is the procedure, and what guidance does it provide?
items.answer: An instrument approach procedure providing descent guidance along a specified track or sector to the visual circling area of an aerodrome. Azimuth guidance is required from the specified radio navigation aid.

departure-briefing.sourceNote: Transcribed from public/source/reference-v7-1/page-34.webp. The source gives a briefing template; these items drill its headings and what belongs under each.

items.prompt: Sample Departure Briefing — what are the five headings?
items.answer: Chart; Flying the Departure; Terrain; Weather; Considerations and Questions

items.prompt: Sample Departure Briefing — what do you brief under Chart?
items.answer: The aerodrome, departure title and index number, and its effective date. Then either the aid tuned, identified and tested to the frequency, or that the SID has been loaded with tracks, distances and heights verified and RAIM available.

items.prompt: Sample Departure Briefing — what do you brief under Flying the Departure and Terrain?
items.answer: Read the initial climb instructions from the chart and discuss the assigned altitude. For terrain, discuss MSAs.

items.prompt: Sample Departure Briefing — what do you brief under Weather?
items.answer: Conditions from AWIS, ATIS or TAF; the effect of wind on tracks; QNH and confirm it is reasonable; and conditions at the destination, confirming they remain suitable.

items.prompt: Sample Departure Briefing — what falls under Considerations and Questions?
items.answer: Relevant chart notes and NOTAMs for the aerodrome and departure; the plan to achieve MSA after an engine failure and the options to return or divert; meteorological conditions and QNH; special considerations such as recent chart changes and traffic; and any further items or questions from the other crew member

items.prompt: Take-off Safety Briefing — which three speeds do you state?
items.answer: VMCA; VR; VYSE

items.prompt: Take-off Safety Briefing — any abnormality before VR?
items.answer: Maintain aircraft control and reject the take-off.

items.prompt: Take-off Safety Briefing — a critical malfunction at or after VR and before VYSE?
items.answer: Maintain aircraft control, then either land because the runway permits, or accelerate to VYSE selecting flap up above 300 feet.

items.prompt: Take-off Safety Briefing — a malfunction above VYSE?
items.answer: Maintain aircraft control, prevent yaw, mixture up, pitch up, power up, gear up, flaps up, then dead leg – dead engine, confirm and feather.

items.prompt: Take-off Safety Briefing — what informs the plan at each particular take-off?
items.answer: Strip length; obstacles; wind for increased climb gradient; terrain and direction of turns; aircraft performance limitations; the type of malfunction that could occur

items.prompt: Take-off Safety Briefing — what do you brief on the basis of meteorological conditions, terrain and facilities?
items.answer: Whether you will circle to land, turning towards the live engine if appropriate, or continue to a nominated alternative; and what you will do if performance is not achieved to climb or maintain level flight.

items.prompt: Sample Approach Briefing — what are the five headings?
items.answer: Chart; Briefing Strip and Terrain; Flying the Approach; Weather; Considerations and Questions

items.prompt: Sample Approach Briefing — what do you brief under Chart?
items.answer: The aerodrome, approach title and index number, and its effective date. Then either the aid tuned, identified and tested to the frequency, or that the approach has been loaded with tracks, distances and heights verified and RAIM available.

items.prompt: Sample Approach Briefing — what do you brief under Briefing Strip and Terrain?
items.answer: Read the first two lines of the Jeppesen Briefing Strip left to right, including MSAs.

items.prompt: Sample Approach Briefing — what do you cover under Flying the Approach?
items.answer: The inbound track and any applicable sector entries or holds; how the approach is flown, with tracks, turns and not-below descent steps; where the runway will be when visual and how you will manoeuvre to land; the missed approach point, the missed approach track and climb altitude; and any aircraft reconfiguration for the missed approach

items.prompt: Sample Approach Briefing — what do you brief under Weather?
items.answer: Expected conditions from AWIS, ATIS or TAF including any difficulty becoming visual; QNH confirmed reasonable; and alternate options with the fuel available to hold or divert.

items.prompt: Sample Approach Briefing — what special considerations does the source list?
items.answer: Relevant NOTAMs for the approach and aerodrome; relevant chart notes; recent changes to the chart; missed approach gradients versus aircraft performance; no-circling areas; runway condition; actions after landing

gradient-nomograph.sourceNote: Transcribed from public/source/reference-v7-1/page-57.webp. Only the equivalences the chart labels explicitly are used; read the figure itself to interpolate.

items.prompt: Gradient Rate Nomograph — what does it give, and from what entering arguments?
items.answer: The climb or descent rate, entered with gradient (as a percentage, ft/NM or degrees) and ground speed.

items.prompt: Gradient Rate Nomograph — what are the ranges of the three scales?
items.answer: Ground speed 60 to 300 knots; climb/descent rate 152 to 3500 fpm; gradient 2.5 to 11.5 per cent, 152 to 700 ft/NM, or 1.5 to 6.5 degrees.

items.answer: Remain in VMC; broadcast intentions prefixed “TRANSMITTING BLIND”; remain VFR in Class G and land at the nearest suitable aerodrome; and report arrival to ATS if on SARTIME or reporting schedules
distractors: Squawk 7600; remain in VMC; land at the nearest suitable aerodrome; and report arrival to ATS
Remain in VMC; squawk 7700; continue to the planned destination; and report arrival to ATS
Remain in VMC; broadcast intentions; continue to the destination; and cancel SARTIME on landing

items.prompt: Communications Failure — in controlled or restricted airspace, or IFR in any airspace: what three actions?

distractors: Squawk 7700; listen out on ATIS; and transmit intentions prefixed “TRANSMITTING BLIND”

Squawk 7600; listen out on the area frequency only; and make no further transmissions

items.prompt: Take-off Minima — for an aeroplane that is not a qualifying multi-engine aeroplane, what are the minima?
items.answer: A cloud ceiling of 300 ft and a visibility of 2000 m
distractors: A cloud ceiling of 300 ft and a visibility of 800 m
A cloud ceiling of 500 ft and a visibility of 2000 m
A cloud ceiling of 200 ft and a visibility of 1500 m

items.prompt: Take-off Minima — for a qualifying multi-engine aeroplane, what are the minima?
items.answer: A visibility of 800 m, with no cloud ceiling requirement. The author notes this can be reduced to 550 m under certain conditions.
distractors: A visibility of 550 m, with no cloud ceiling requirement
A cloud ceiling of 300 ft and a visibility of 800 m
A visibility of 2000 m, with no cloud ceiling requirement

items.prompt: Take-off Minima — when must a pilot in command not commence a take-off?
items.answer: If the meteorological conditions are less than the take-off minima for the aircraft; or if the conditions that would exist on returning to land because of engine failure are not at or above the landing minima for an IAP the pilot can conduct, or such as to allow a visual approach for the return
distractors: If the meteorological conditions are less than the take-off minima for the aircraft, only
If the conditions are less than the landing minima at the destination
If the conditions are less than the alternate minima at the departure aerodrome

items.prompt: Take-off Minima — what crewing makes an aeroplane a qualifying multi-engine aeroplane?
items.answer: Operated by at least 2 pilots; or by 1 pilot if piston or turboprop powered and fitted with operative autofeather; or by 1 pilot if turbojet powered
distractors: Operated by at least 2 pilots in all cases
Operated by 1 pilot if fitted with an autopilot, regardless of engine type
Operated by at least 2 pilots, or by 1 pilot if turbojet powered

items.prompt: Take-off Minima — what performance must a qualifying multi-engine aeroplane have after an engine failure?
items.answer: It must be capable of maintaining terrain clearance until reaching the minimum height for IFR flight.
distractors: It must be capable of maintaining 500 ft per minute climb to the MSA
It must be capable of returning to land at the departure aerodrome
It must be capable of maintaining terrain clearance until reaching the circling minima

items.prompt: Landing Minima — for an RNP APCH-LNAV/VNAV, RNP APCH-LPV or precision approach, the minimum altitude must not be below whichever is highest of what?
items.answer: The DA or DH on the instrument approach chart for the IAP being conducted; the relevant minima in the AFM; or the relevant minima in the operator's exposition or operations manual
distractors: The DA or DH on the chart; the MDA for the circling procedure; or the operator's minima
The DA or DH on the chart; the LSALT for the final segment; or the AFM minima
The DA or DH on the chart only

items.prompt: Landing Minima — the minimum visibility must not be below whichever is highest of what?
items.answer: The RVR or visibility on the instrument approach chart; the relevant minima in the AFM; or the relevant minima in the operator's exposition or operations manual
distractors: The RVR on the chart only
The RVR or visibility on the chart; the alternate minima; or the operator's minima
The RVR or visibility on the chart; the AFM minima; or 800 m, whichever is greatest in all cases

items.prompt: Landing Minima — when does a minimum visibility of 1200 m apply?
